body:
* High priority threads are use exclusively by high priority tasks.
* Low priority threads are shared be high priority and low priority tasks.
* A task that is "promoted" is moved from the front of the low priority queue to the back of the main queue when a low priority slot is freed up. The LP task still has to wait for all the HP tasks to finish.

"Threads will be reserved for low-priority tasks" means that those threads are usable *only* by low-priority threads and not by high-priority threads. That's not what happens.

body:
That's a good point. I concede that "reserve" is the wrong choice of words. 

However, the rest of my point still stands. If there are no high priority tasks then low priority tasks can run on all the threads. 

Here is a quote from RandomShaper (the author of this system):

>There's the concept of low and high priority tasks, and a configuration setting about the ratio of threads that may run low prio tasks. The semantics are that high prio tasks can run on any thread. Low prio tasks can run on any thread that is either idle (i.e., there are no outstanding high prio tasks) or if the low prio workers ratio has not been reached yet.

So maybe a better way of explaining things is:
1. High priority tasks can run on any thread
2. Low priority tasks can only run on low priority threads when there are high priority tasks in the queue
3. If there are no high priority tasks in the queue, low priority threads can run everywhere. 

Alternatively, from the perspective of threads:
1. High priority threads draw exclusively from the high priority tasks queue until it is empty, then they can take low priority tasks
2. Low priority threads draw from the low priority task queue until the low priority worker ratio is reached or until the queue is empty.

I tested it on the new 4.5.0 release just to be sure.  Same behavior. 

Upon reflection: The way I described it is how it works, but there is another discussion to be had about whether that's how it *should* work.

The default is low-priority, and by default low-priority can never use more than 30% of CPU time with the remainder being reserved *just in case* a high-priority task comes along. In a video game context, I would by default want my Worker Threads use as much CPU as they can without affecting the main thread.  
When using WTP to speed up processing, I'd want to either use high-priority threads to utilize all cores or set `low_priority_thread_ratio = 0.99` to utilize (n-1) cores.  
The low-priority threads with default settings are suitable for background tasks where I don't need the result any time soon.

So we have to either explain to the user that any task that the main thread is waiting for should be a high-priority thread, or change the method so `high_priority := true` is the default. If you're using low-priority threads and your main thread is stalled waiting on them, you're doing it wrong.

Does that make sense?

body:
I re-read the code again, and the number of low priority tasks is a hard limit.
A low priority task is added to the main queue in one of 3 situations:
* there are fewer than `max_low_priority_threads` low priority tasks when the task is created
* a low priority task finishes
* a low priority task waits (this is the thing that confused me previously)

I can think of the following explanations for the issue you are observing:
* The low priority tasks are finishing or entering the wait state so quickly that they appear to be running in parallel
* The tasks in question are not `low_priority` in the sense of WorkerThreadPool.add_task() (they might be `low priority` in the OS sense?)
* The threads you see are not managed by the WorkerThreadPool singleton.

But without seeing the code that caused the situation I can't tell what exactly is happening.

All I know for sure is that the WorkerThreadPool singleton, when called from gdScript, behaves as I described.
